summary: Matthias Loibl from Polar Signals presents their continuous profiling platform extended to GPUs. Profiling, dating back to the 1970s, captures memory, CPU, and GPU time spent, instruction usage, and function call frequency and duration to improve performance and save costs. Two profiling approaches exist: tracing (records every event, high cost, high data volume) and sampled profiling (samples at intervals like 100 times per second, yielding less than 1% CPU overhead and ~4MB memory overhead). Polar Signals uses sampled profiling via Linux eBPF, requiring no application instrumentation—one process profiles all applications. After 3-4 years of CPU and memory profiling work, Polar Signals launched a GPU profiling preview earlier this year. GPU metrics are collected through Nvidia NVML, including node and per-process utilization, memory utilization, clock speed, power utilization with power limit, temperature (with throttling risk at ~80°C), and PCIe throughput. These metrics correlate with CPU flame charts to diagnose GPU underutilization—often caused by the CPU busy loading data rather than keeping the GPU busy. The platform works with compiled languages (Rust, C) and interpreted languages (Python, Ruby, JVM). A newly announced GPU time profiling feature tells the Linux kernel to report start and end times of CUDA kernels, enabling measurement of actual GPU execution time per function. Deployment options include a binary, Docker container, or Kubernetes DaemonSet with manifest YAML and a token. Customer Turbo Puffer is integrating GPU profiling for their vector engine.

sections.title: Introduction to Profiling
sections.summary: Profiling has existed since the 1970s and captures memory, CPU, and GPU time spent, instruction usage, and function call frequency and duration. It serves performance engineering to improve performance and save money—e.g., a 10% software improvement could let you turn off 10% of servers. Two approaches exist: tracing (records every event, high cost, high data volume) and sampled profiling (samples at intervals, lower overhead, suitable for continuous use).

sections.title: Sampled Profiling with eBPF
sections.summary: Sampled profiling at 100 times per second yields less than 1% CPU overhead and ~4MB memory overhead. While it misses some events, always-on sampling eventually captures most relevant stacks. Polar Signals uses Linux eBPF, profiling all applications without requiring any instrumentation—start one process and it profiles everything. This enables production profiling, which is critical since a developer's machine is not the production environment.

sections.title: Speaker Introduction and GPU Profiling Preview
sections.summary: Matthias Loibl, Director of Polar Signals, flew in from Berlin, Germany. He is a maintainer of the Prometheus Operator and the open-source version of the profiling work discussed. After 3-4 years of CPU and memory profiling, Polar Signals launched a GPU profiling preview earlier this year, using Nvidia NVML to extract GPU metrics.

sections.title: GPU Metrics Collection
sections.summary: The platform collects GPU node and per-process utilization (blue and orange lines), memory utilization, clock speed, power utilization with power limit (dashed line), temperature, and PCIe throughput. Temperature matters because sustained ~80°C causes significant GPU throttling. PCIe throughput (10MB/s in example) reveals whether the workload is bound by CPU-GPU data transfer.

sections.title: Correlating GPU Metrics with CPU Profiles
sections.summary: GPU metrics are correlated with CPU profiles collected via eBPF. Users can drag and select a time range to view a flame chart showing what the CPU is doing when the GPU is underutilized. Often the CPU is busy loading data (e.g., Python calling CUDA functions) rather than keeping the GPU busy.

sections.title: Language Support
sections.summary: The platform works with Python, Rust, and any compiled language, plus interpreted languages like Ruby, Python, and JVM. While the conference focus is GPUs, the profiling applies to web servers, databases, and vector databases as well.

sections.title: GPU Time Profiling Announcement
sections.summary: Newly announced GPU time profiling tells the Linux kernel to report the start and end times of CUDA kernels, measuring actual GPU execution duration per function. A real-world example shows CPU stack frames (Python to libcudart) with GPU time as leaf nodes, width representing GPU time. Colors represent different binaries (e.g., blue for Python).

sections.title: Getting Started and Conclusion
sections.summary: Deployment via binary, Docker, or Kubernetes DaemonSet with manifest YAML and token. Existing CPU/memory profiling customers, including Turbo Puffer (vector engine), are integrating GPU profiling. Booth offers: first 10 signups get 2 hours free consultation; discounts available for Series A startups.
